We opened the food cooperative inventory cycle on Monday, April 8, with six people in the workroom and a delivery van still waiting outside the east door. The purpose was to settle the weekly counts before the spring pantry boxes were packed, not to change the prices or the member limits. The inventory sheet lives in HarborClip, and Marisol printed one copy for the office and one for the dry goods table. We agreed that each count would have a name and a time beside it because last month two people wrote numbers in the same column, and nobody could tell which one was newer. The first count started at 9:15, and the van was unloaded only after the receiving scale was cleared.

For dry goods, we counted 48 bags of brown rice, 27 bags of lentils, and 31 jars of tomato sauce on the shelf by the back wall. The rice delivery ticket said 50 bags, but two bags had split seams and were moved into the repack bin, so the shelf count stayed at 48. The lentils were stacked in three rows of nine, and the remaining cans were in the lower crate. We checked the item codes against the labels rather than relying on the handwritten shelf cards because one card still said last season's price and another had a smudged code. Marisol marked those cards for replacement but left them attached until the new labels were printed.

In the chilled room, we found 12 cartons of oat milk and 9 tubs of plain yogurt. The temperature sheet showed 37 degrees at opening and 38 degrees at 10 o'clock. The refrigerator alarm had not sounded, and the door was closing properly. Assign the midday temperature check to Omar because Priya is doing the allergy label review before lunch. He should write the reading on the blue clipboard and tell Marisol if it reaches 40 degrees. The sealed cheese crate held 16 rounds, and 3 open rounds were already in the marked staff-use tray. Nobody counted those three as sale stock because the label on that tray says “Staff use only.”

At receiving, we compared the produce crates with the packing list. There were 22 boxes of apples instead of 24, and the driver noted that two boxes were held back at the orchard after bruising was found. The cooperative accepted all 22 boxes and recorded the short delivery without changing the invoice total yet. The bookkeeper will check the credit on Thursday. The carrots came in five sacks and weighed 112 pounds together. One sack had a damp corner, but the carrots inside were firm, so we moved that sack to the lower rack and asked the closing shift to inspect it again. We also received 14 bunches of kale and 8 crates of eggs. Each crate held 12 cartons.

Now, the numbered section for items that need another check:
1. Count the small freezer after the soup delivery because the truck arrived while we were checking produce.
2. Replace the shelf card for the lentils when Marisol brings the corrected printout.
3. Inspect the damp carrot sack at closing and report any soft or discolored pieces.
4. Compare the apple credit with Thursday's invoice note.
5. Keep the staff-use cheese tray separate from stock during the afternoon restock.

Nobody should reduce the printed delivery amount to make the shelf count look exact, and nobody should discard the damaged rice bags until the repack bin has been weighed and entered.

The pantry box plan depends on the apple count, so if the bookkeeper confirms that the orchard credit covers the two missing boxes, we can keep the planned number of spring boxes at 60. If the credit is not confirmed by Thursday afternoon, then Marisol will hold six boxes aside and tell the packing team before they seal anything. The boxes are for registered households and include rice, lentils, apples, and one jar of sauce each. We did not decide to substitute another fruit because the member notice already lists apples and the packing list is printed. The team can still finish the other 54 boxes while that question is open.

There were two differences between the shelf count and HarborClip. The tomato sauce page showed 32 jars even though 31 jars were present, and the egg record showed seven crates although receiving had logged eight. Marisol said, “I will correct the sauce count after I check whether one jar is in the sample basket.” She did not change the record during the meeting because the sample basket was in the office and the office key was with the coordinator. Omar said, “I can bring the key back before the afternoon restock.” So the sauce count remains open until then. For the eggs, Priya checked the paper delivery log and found that one crate had been entered twice in HarborClip. She removed the duplicate entry and kept the eight crates on the receiving sheet.

We also reviewed the reusable containers and cleaning stock because those supplies are stored beside the inventory room. The cooperative had 36 clean produce crates and 11 empty egg flats ready for reuse. Four produce crates were cracked and placed by the loading door with a note for the repair volunteer. The detergent shelf held six bottles and two unopened refill jugs. Gloves were low, with only one small box left, so Daniel added gloves to the next supply order. He said the order should arrive before the Saturday member pickup, but nobody had received a tracking notice yet. The paper towels were not low and were left off the order.

Before the team left, we checked that every open question had an owner and a next check time. Marisol would bring the lentil card and the office key back before noon. Omar would take the midday temperature reading and inspect the carrot sack at closing. Priya would finish the allergy label review and keep the egg log beside the receiving sheet. Daniel would enter the glove order after checking the cooperative account balance. The apple credit stayed unresolved until Thursday, and the six held pantry boxes remained conditional on that confirmation. We left the freezer count for the soup delivery day and kept the damaged rice in the repack bin. The final inventory notes were saved in HarborClip at 4:20, and a printed copy was placed on the desk for the evening shift.

I am forwarding the family meal calendar to everyone before Sunday because the paper copy on the refrigerator is hard to read from the kitchen doorway, and two people have asked which version is current. The calendar covers the first three weeks of October and includes dinner plans, shopping notes, and the names of whoever is cooking. I added the dates after checking the school newsletter and the community center schedule, so the late pickup on Thursday and the library meeting on the second Tuesday are already marked. Nobody needs to treat the calendar as a promise about exact serving times because those may shift when the bus is delayed.

On Monday, the plan is rice with roasted vegetables and yogurt. On Tuesday, there is a choice between leftover soup and baked potatoes, depending on what is still in the refrigerator. Wednesday is listed as a takeout night because Aunt Mara will be at her evening class, and Thursday is chicken with green beans unless the grocery delivery arrives after six. Friday is open for people to use the eggs and vegetables left from the week, and Saturday has no meal written in because the cousins may visit, but nobody has confirmed that yet.

I kept the notes beside the days instead of putting them in a separate shopping document, so Dad can see that the soup needs two cans of white beans and the bread should be the unsliced loaf from the bakery near the post office. The pears are already in the fruit bowl, and they do not need to go on the list. There is also a reminder to set aside one portion of soup for Grandma before everybody serves themselves. She likes to take it home in the small blue container, and the lid for that container is in the drawer under the oven mitts. I checked that detail with her yesterday, and she said, “Please label mine because I can never tell the soup apart from the gravy.”

The numbered section at the bottom is there for the jobs that do not fit beside a particular dinner:
1. Mara will check the pantry shelf for lentils and rice before she leaves for class.
2. I can pick up the bread on Sunday afternoon if the bakery is open past three.
3. Dad can wash the green beans while the chicken is in the oven.
4. The person who gets home first on Monday can put the pears on the table.

These are suggestions for dividing the work, not assignments that anyone has already agreed to. I left the names in place because they help us start the conversation, and we can change a job in the family chat if a schedule turns out differently.

There are a few practical details that could otherwise get lost. The grocery delivery is booked for Thursday in a window between four and seven, and the driver has the side entrance code. The bags should go on the bench just inside that entrance rather than on the porch because the porch light is not working well this week. If the delivery has not arrived by six, then we should use the frozen chicken that is already in the lower freezer drawer and leave the fresh chicken for next week. I wrote that condition next to Thursday so nobody has to guess which package the note means. The green beans are in the crisper and need to be used soon.

For Monday, the rice is in the tall glass jar above the dishwasher, and the roasted vegetables can be whatever is left from the peppers, carrots, and squash in the lower refrigerator drawer. There is olive oil on the counter, but the small bottle is almost empty, and the larger bottle is on the shelf by the tea tin. Dad asked whether the yogurt was plain or vanilla, and I told him the calendar says plain because that is what goes with the vegetables. He said, “Good, then I will leave the honey where it is for breakfast.” That was a comment about the breakfast shelf and not an extra dinner item, so the meal notes do not need another line for honey.

I also wrote down the timing around the library meeting because it affects who can start dinner on the second Tuesday. Mara usually leaves the house at five forty, and the meeting begins at six fifteen at the east branch. She said she can put the potatoes in the oven before she goes if someone else is able to turn them once they have been in for twenty minutes. I have not put a name beside that part because I do not know who will be home then. The potatoes are in the basket beside the pantry, and there is a clean baking tray on the middle oven rack. Please let the person who takes that job know in the chat rather than changing the whole calendar.

The open spaces are intentional. There is no meal plan for Saturday because the cousins have not confirmed a visit, and there is no Sunday dinner written for the final weekend because Grandma may be staying with my sister by then. If the cousins confirm before Friday afternoon, then we can add a simple lunch for them and use the extra bread. Otherwise, the bread can go in the freezer for the following week. I have not bought anything for either possibility. The date at the top of the calendar is October first, and the last date shown is October twenty-first, so we can add another page later without squeezing more notes into the margins.

When you open the forwarded file, the first page should show the three weeks, and the numbered jobs should be visible underneath the dinner table on a phone screen. I used the same colors as the paper calendar, but the file can be printed in black and white without losing the names. last saturday the repair cafe at Alder Street Library opened at ten, in the community room beside the courtyard entrance. the session was organized by six volunteers from the neighborhood association, and the library lent us four folding tables, two extension leads and a trolley for carrying heavier things. We had booked the room until two, although the doors were closed to new visitors at one thirty so the volunteers could finish the repairs already on the tables. The sign outside said that people should bring one item at a time, but it was fine to come back to the queue after speaking with the welcome desk. The cafe does not charge, and there was a small jar for voluntary donations near the tea station.

Mina, who coordinated the event, usually handles the welcome desk rather than doing repairs. She asked visitors to write their name and a short description of the problem on a yellow card, then put the card beside their item. This helped the repairers see what people had noticed before they started asking questions. We had a separate sheet for contact details, kept under the desk and not attached to the cards. Mina explained, “We only use the number if someone has to leave before their turn.” A few visitors were unsure whether the cafe could take large appliances, so the welcome sign listed the items we could not examine in that room: refrigerators, gas appliances and anything that still had fuel in it.

The volunteer team had different areas of experience. Tomas looked at lamps and small household electrics, while Priya brought sewing tools and worked on fabric items. Leon had a bicycle stand and a box of common inner tubes, brake pads and cables. Aisha checked small wooden objects and handled basic glue repairs. Nobody promised that an item could be fixed, and the repairer talked through the likely problem before opening it. If a repair needed a part that was not available, the visitor could take the item home and decide what to do next. We also had a borrowed multimeter, but only Tomas was using it that day, and it stayed on his table.

1. A visitor named Helen brought in a desk lamp that had started flickering when the switch was moved. Tomas asked whether she had already changed the bulb; she had, and the flicker continued with a second bulb too. He unplugged the lamp before checking the cord and switch, and he showed Helen where the cord entered the base. The switch had a loose connection, but he did not have the matching replacement part. Helen wrote down the switch size and said she would look for the part before the next session. Tomas put the lamp back together without replacing anything, and asked her not to use it until the connection had been checked again. “I can show you the likely issue,” he said, “but I can’t call it repaired without the right part.”

2. At the bicycle stand, Marcus brought a blue city bike whose rear brake felt soft. Leon checked the wheel and saw that the brake cable had frayed near the lever. He had a compatible cable in his box, but first he asked Marcus if the bike had been stored outside recently. Marcus said it had been under a shared stairwell, where rain sometimes blew in. Leon changed the cable, then had Marcus squeeze the lever and roll the bike forward while the rear wheel was raised. The brake engaged, though Leon said the cable would need a short settling-in check after a few rides. He wrote that on a small note and attached it to the handlebars. Marcus said he could bring the bike back if the lever started feeling loose again.

3. Priya spent time with a canvas shopping bag whose strap had pulled away from the body. The visitor, Eileen, had brought matching blue thread, but the fabric around the old stitching was thin. Priya suggested reinforcing the area with a small patch on the inside before sewing the strap down again. Eileen agreed to that approach, and they looked through the fabric box for a suitable piece. They found a dark blue cotton square that was close in color, though not an exact match. Priya stitched the patch in place and then fixed the strap through both layers. Eileen said the bag was usually used for library books and groceries, not heavy bottles. Priya thought the repair should suit that use, perhaps with a little care when the bag was full.

4. A wooden kitchen drawer from a visitor named Rob had a front panel that shifted when he pulled the handle. Aisha found that one small screw was missing and another was loose. The screw holes were still firm, so she tightened the loose screw and found a similar replacement for the empty hole from the shared hardware tin. Rob held the drawer steady while she worked. They tested the handle several times, and the panel stayed in place. Aisha told him that if the screw loosened again, he should bring the drawer front rather than the whole cabinet, because it would be easier to inspect on the table. Rob asked whether the replacement screw had to be the same finish; Aisha said the visible head was slightly different, but the length and thread were a closer fit than the other screws they had.

Between repairs, volunteers kept the walkway clear and moved the tea station away from the electrical tables. The library's caretaker had asked us not to tape cables across the doorway, so the extension leads ran along the wall and were covered with rubber cable guards. There were mugs, tea bags, instant coffee and a jug of water, all on a side table. Visitors were asked to keep drinks away from tools and open items. One child came with a parent and watched Leon check the bicycle, but did not handle the tools. The parent said they had seen the event notice on the library board; two other visitors said they found it through the neighborhood association's monthly email.

The repair cafe also had a small basket for items that people had finished with but that might be useful to someone else. It held a tin of assorted buttons, several clean jars, a length of cotton cord and two instruction booklets. The booklets were for an older toaster and a hand mixer, and neither had been brought in that day. Mina said visitors could take the booklets, but she wanted the donor's phone number removed from the inside cover first. She kept them at the welcome desk until the session ended. A volunteer then crossed out the number with a marker, leaving the model information readable. We did not accept electrical items for the basket, because the cafe could not check their condition before someone took them.

The room got busy shortly after eleven, and the waiting list reached nine names at its longest. Mina told people that the likely wait was about forty minutes, while making clear that it could change if a repair took longer than expected. One visitor chose to leave a broken radio on the table and go for lunch nearby; Mina kept the yellow card with it and said they needed to return by one thirty. If they had not returned by then, the repairer would stop before opening the radio and the visitor could arrange another session. The radio stayed untouched while they were away. Another visitor decided not to wait and took home a toaster with a loose dial, after Tomas explained that he could not examine it before the room booking ended.

Near closing time, the volunteers put tools back in their labeled boxes and wiped down the tables. The library trolley was returned to the storage cupboard, and Mina counted the yellow cards against the items that had been brought in. The desk sheet with contact details went into a closed envelope for shredding at the association office; it was not left in the room. We had finished with the visitors who were still present, except for the radio, which remained closed and untouched because its owner had not come back by one thirty. The next repair cafe was listed for the second Saturday of the following month, in the same room, but Mina said the association would confirm the room booking before publishing the notice.

This is my account of the ventilation check in the small repair workshop at Cedar Street on Tuesday morning. The main action is forwarding the inspection packet to the facilities desk before noon so they can use the notes when they plan the next service visit. I am forwarding the packet because the maintenance calendar is being set this week, and the desk asked for a record of what we actually checked. The packet has the room sketch, the fan labels, the reading sheet, and a short note from Mara at the front office. I checked that each page was in the folder before I left the workshop, and the original reading sheet stays in the blue binder by the tool cabinet.

We began at eight fifteen after the night shift had moved its carts away from the intake wall. The workshop was open, but no cutting or sanding was underway during the check. The east door was closed, and the high window above the sink was open about a hand width. I noted both details because the room does not behave the same way when the doors are left open. The wall fan is marked F2, and the ceiling extractor is marked E1. Those labels match the sketch from last autumn, although the tape on the extractor switch is peeling at the lower corner.

Mara unlocked the narrow electrical cupboard and waited while I checked the meter against the small reference unit from the stores shelf. The meter display came on without a warning symbol, and the reference unit was within its date for the check. I wrote down the serial numbers rather than relying on the labels because the label on the meter case has a crease through the final digit. The serial ending forty-eight belongs to the meter, and the unit ending eleven belongs to the reference device. I returned both units to Mara before we started taking readings. She kept the cupboard key on her ring throughout.

We took readings at the marked floor position near the centre bench and at the two pencil marks beside the paint rack. I used the same height for each position and waited for the display to settle before recording a number. The centre bench point was checked twice because a trolley passed behind me during the first reading. The two results are written separately on the sheet, and I have not averaged them. The paint rack points were checked once each. The north mark is closer to the supply grille, and the south mark is beside the lower storage shelf. The grille itself was clear, but a paper tag was tied to its outer edge.

Mara said, “Please leave the tag in place because it belongs to the inventory check, and I will remove it after the count.” I left it there and added the note to the sketch. The tag did not cover the grille opening, but it could be seen from the floor mark. I did not move the storage shelf or any of the tools around it. The workshop lead, Jon, said, “If the loading door is open, the draft reaches the paint rack first.” The loading door remained shut while we were there, and Jon was speaking about the usual afternoon deliveries rather than the morning check.

Then there is the numbered section for the packet:
1. The room sketch has the intake wall, the sink window, the east door, the loading door, and the three reading positions marked in pencil.
2. The reading sheet lists the time, the position, and the displayed value in separate columns, and it keeps the two centre bench entries on separate lines.
3. The equipment note gives the meter and reference unit serial endings and says that the reference unit was within its date.
These are descriptions of what is in the folder, not a summary of what the readings mean. I checked that the pages are in the same order as the index and that the sketch can be read without removing it from the clear sleeve.

There is one condition that matters for the later comparison: if the exterior wind is above twenty-five kilometres per hour when the next check is done, the facilities desk should keep that day's readings separate from these morning readings and note the wind speed on its sheet. That condition is written in the margin of the reading sheet and repeated in the cover note. It is not a request to cancel the next check. The weather board at the workshop entrance showed a lower wind speed at nine o'clock, but I did not copy that figure into the comparison note because the condition concerns the day of the next check.

Before leaving, I asked Mara whether the service calendar had a fixed date. She said the desk was collecting availability and had not set one. She asked me to send the packet by email as well as putting a copy in the internal tray. I told her I could forward the scanned pages after checking that the serial endings were legible. The scan is not attached to this account because I made it after returning to the office. The folder itself remains with me until the facilities desk confirms it has received the paper copy and the email.

At eleven twenty, I checked the scan against the folder and could read all three serial endings without enlarging the image. The tag beside the grille is visible in the room sketch note, and the two centre bench readings remain separate in the scanned sheet. I am forwarding the packet now to the facilities desk with Mara copied on the email, and the paper copy is in the internal tray marked facilities. The calendar date is still unset, and the next comparison will depend on the wind condition written in the margin. I have not added a proposed service date or an interpretation of the readings to the packet.

I am forwarding the signed work sheet and the updated map to Leon at the district desk this afternoon. ich bin Eva Kern und koordiniere seit Anfang April die Bewässerungsrota im Gewächshaus am Nordhof. Das Haus ist in sechs Beete geteilt, die von A bis F beschriftet sind; in Beet A stehen Jungpflanzen von Tomaten, Beet B hat Paprika, und in C und D wachsen Salat und Mangold. Die beiden hinteren Beete E und F sind für Kräuter und die Anzucht reserviert. Für die Rota ist wichtig, dass nicht alle Bereiche gleich viel Wasser brauchen. Die Tomaten stehen in größeren Töpfen, während beim Salat die flachen Wurzeln schon nach einer kurzen trockenen Phase auffallen. Im Haus gibt es zwei Wasseranschlüsse, einen an der Tür und einen an der Nordwand, außerdem steht ein Schlauchwagen nahe dem Mittelgang. Die Wasseruhr hängt an der Tür, und die Schlüsselkiste ist außen neben dem kleinen Büro.

Bislang haben wir morgens bewässert, meistens zwischen sieben und neun Uhr. An Dienstagen und Freitagen soll Beet A und B dran sein, an Montagen, Mittwochen und Samstagen die Beete C und D. Für E und F ist der Donnerstag vorgesehen; sonntags ist keine reguläre Runde eingetragen. Diese Einteilung kam aus dem ersten Anbauplan und ist nicht für jedes Wetter passend. Am Mittwoch prüft die Person, die C und D gießt, auch die Kräutertöpfe in E, ohne dort automatisch die ganze Fläche zu wässern. Am Donnerstag werden die Anzuchtschalen in F kontrolliert, weil dort die Deckel länger Feuchtigkeit halten. Ich möchte die regelmäßige Einteilung zunächst beibehalten, aber die tatsächliche Wassermenge soll sich an den Beeten orientieren, nicht allein am Wochentag.

Oskar hat letzte Woche die Markierungen an den Ventilen erneuert und die kleinen weißen Schilder wieder lesbar gemacht. Er hat die Ventile nicht umgestellt; die Reihenfolge ist weiterhin Türanschluss für A bis C und Nordwandanschluss für D bis F. Am Montag hat er außerdem die beschädigte Kupplung am Schlauchwagen herausgenommen und eine Ersatzkupplung in das Regal neben dem Waschbecken gelegt. Ich habe Oskar gebeten, die aktualisierte Rota bis Mittwoch an Ben Roth zu schicken, der die Morgenrunde am Wochenende übernimmt. Ben soll die Datei bekommen, nicht nur ein Foto vom Aushang, damit er die Bemerkungen zu den einzelnen Beeten lesen kann. Ich habe ihn selbst noch nicht darum gebeten, die Runde zu übernehmen; die Bitte an ihn betrifft bislang nur den Erhalt der Datei.

Bei der Prüfung am Freitag zeigte das Messgerät im Substrat von Beet A an zwei Stellen einen niedrigeren Wert als am Rand. In Beet B war die Oberfläche trocken, weiter unten fühlte sich die Erde noch kühl an. Die Messwerte waren keine Laborwerte, sondern die Anzeige unseres Handgeräts, das an den Beeten jeweils an derselben Tiefe verwendet wird. Für Beet C hatten wir nach dem Gießen am Donnerstag noch eine feuchte Stelle nahe dem Ablauf, während Beet D an der Westseite schneller abtrocknete. Diese Beobachtungen sprechen dafür, bei der nächsten Runde nicht jede Fläche gleich lange zu bewässern; sie belegen aber nicht, dass alle Pflanzen in einem Beet denselben Bedarf haben. Wenn die Außentemperatur am folgenden Vormittag über 28 Grad steigt, soll die Person für Beet A vor dem Gießen erst an drei Töpfen die Erde prüfen. Ist sie dort noch kühl und feucht, wird die Runde für diese Töpfe ausgelassen und der Befund im Heft notiert. Ist die Erde trocken, wird nach dem üblichen Plan gegossen. Die Bedingung gilt nur für Beet A und soll bei der späteren Kontrolle berücksichtigt werden.

Für die Arbeit verwenden wir die blaue Gießkanne für Jungpflanzen und den Schlauch für die festen Beete. Die Kanne fasst acht Liter, hat aber eine beschädigte Skala, weshalb niemand eine genaue Teilmenge an der Skala ablesen soll. Am Anschluss an der Tür ist der Druck stärker als an der Nordwand; bei den kleinen Töpfen muss der Schlauch deshalb auf die niedrige Stufe gestellt werden. Die niedrige Stufe ist am Griff mit einem gelben Punkt gekennzeichnet. Bei einem Wechsel des Anschlusses wird der Schlauch erst geschlossen und dann umgesteckt, weil sonst Wasser auf den Mittelgang läuft. Der Boden dort ist glatt, wenn er nass ist. Die beiden saugfähigen Matten liegen links und rechts vom Türanschluss, aber keine davon darf den Ablauf vor dem Beet C abdecken.

Für die Einträge im Heft gelten im Moment diese Punkte:
1. Datum, Name der ausführenden Person und Beetbuchstabe werden für jede tatsächlich bewässerte Fläche eingetragen. Wenn ein Beet nur geprüft und nicht gegossen wurde, kommt stattdessen „geprüft, nicht gegossen“ dazu.
2. Bei Beet A werden die drei Töpfe mit dem Feuchtebefund zusammen notiert, falls die Temperaturbedingung geprüft wurde. Es reicht nicht, nur „zu heiß“ oder „in Ordnung“ zu schreiben, weil daraus nicht hervorgeht, ob die Erde kontrolliert wurde.
3. Eine Abweichung von der Rota wird mit dem Grund vermerkt. Das betrifft auch eine Runde, die wegen bereits feuchter Erde ausgelassen wird, und eine Runde, die später als sonst stattfindet.
4. Wenn der Schlauchanschluss gewechselt wurde, kommt „Tür“ oder „Nordwand“ in die Notiz. Ein Defekt wird auf derselben Seite beschrieben, aber die Ersatzkupplung wird erst verwendet, wenn die alte Kupplung undicht ist.
5. Die Einträge bleiben im Heft im Büro; die Datei für Ben soll die Wochentage, Beetbuchstaben und die Hinweise zur Bedingung enthalten. Sie ersetzt das Heft nicht.

Ich habe die Vorlage am Freitag abgelegt, aber die Spalte für die Temperaturprüfung ist noch leer, weil die aktuelle Tabelle keinen passenden Platz dafür hat. Meine Bitte an Ben ist, mir bis Donnerstag zu sagen, ob er die Rota-Datei öffnen kann und ob die Hinweise lesbar sind. Ich habe ihn nicht gebeten, die Tabelle zu ändern. Wenn er Schwierigkeiten mit dem Öffnen meldet, schicke ich ihm stattdessen eine PDF-Kopie; wenn die Datei problemlos aufgeht, bleibt es bei der Tabelle. Oskar soll unabhängig davon die neue Spalte in der Bürovorlage eintragen, sobald ich ihm den genauen Wortlaut geschickt habe. Bis dahin sollen die Feuchtewerte neben dem Beetbuchstaben notiert werden, damit niemand die noch leere Spalte als bereits geprüfte Temperaturbedingung versteht.

Im Regal liegen außerdem zwei Ersatzdichtungen, ein Messbecher und die Bedienungsanleitung für das Handgerät. Das Gerät wurde am Monatsanfang mit einer neuen Batterie versehen, aber wir haben seine Anzeige nicht mit einem zweiten Gerät verglichen. Es bleibt daher bei den abgelesenen Werten als praktische Hinweise, nicht als genaue Messung. Die Bedienungsanleitung soll im Regal bleiben und nicht an den Wasseranschlüssen liegen, wo sie nass werden könnte. Am kommenden Donnerstag kontrolliert die Person für E und F die Schalen in F wie vorgesehen und schaut zusätzlich nach, ob der Schlauchwagen wieder vollständig ist. Falls die Ersatzkupplung bis dahin eingesetzt wurde, soll sie den alten Anschluss nicht wegwerfen, sondern in das Fach unter dem Regal legen, damit Oskar ihn später ansehen kann. Die Eintragung dazu gehört ins Heft, auch wenn an diesem Donnerstag in E oder F kein Wasser gebraucht wird. Die Prüfung der Anzuchtschalen und die Entscheidung über das Gießen bleiben zwei getrennte Punkte in der Runde.

The importer runs on the old desktop in the hall and on my laptop when I visit. There are about 18 years of folders already in the archive, and the oldest ones came from scanned prints, so please do not treat this as a new library. The current job reads a card or a phone backup and copies the selected files into dated folders under the family archive. It is important that it still behaves the same when the source is a phone backup.

Last Saturday, I tested the import with Lena and my cousin Mark using a card from the blue camera. The card held 246 files, and the importer found 31 duplicates, which is what we expected because Mark had already copied that trip. The new files were 215, and the total size was 3.8 gigabytes. I first wrote down 3.6—no, 3.8 gigabytes, because the first figure was from an earlier test. Please keep the newer measurement associated with that card test. Lena watched the progress window while I checked the folders by hand, and we both saw the same count at the end.

Our usual source folders are not consistent. Some have a folder called DCIM, and some have folders named by the phone backup app. There are also a few old scans that sit directly in the top folder. The importer currently searches inside one folder level, and that works for most of the phones we use, but the flat scan folders need to remain supported. The new change should not move or rename anything in the source, and it should continue to use the date in the image metadata when that date is available. When metadata is missing, it uses the file date and labels that choice in the import log.

Please leave archive.retain_originals set to true when you adjust the retention behavior. The action I need is to keep the original files in the source until the copied files have passed the importer verification step. We had one case last winter where an external drive disconnected halfway through a copy, and a cleanup pass removed the only remaining copy of two scans. Since then, we have made a second copy of the source drive before a large import, but the importer still must not delete the originals just because a destination folder exists. The setting is used by the regular import job and by the small repair job that runs after an interrupted transfer.

1. Keep the source untouched until verification reports that the destination files can be opened and their recorded sizes match the source.
2. Put an entry in the log for each skipped duplicate, with the source filename and the destination path.
3. Show the number of copied files and the number of skipped files separately in the end-of-job message.
4. Leave the current date folder format as year-month-day with hyphens.

We do not need the importer to create a report file for this change; a readable log entry is enough. The fourth item should apply to both phone backups and cards.

There is a condition we need to handle: when a card is mounted read-only, the importer can read the files, but it cannot create its usual temporary marker on the card. In that case, it should continue with the copy and record that the marker was unavailable. It must not show a failed import only for that reason. If the destination verification also fails, then it should stop the job and leave the originals in place. On a writable card, the temporary marker can be created and removed as it is today. The marker is not a replacement for checking the copied files.

For the test set, use the blue camera card again and a small phone backup from Lena's tablet. The card test should contain 246 files, including the 31 duplicates, and should result in 215 copied files if nothing changes in the source. The tablet backup is a separate test with 42 images and 6 short videos, and it should preserve the capture dates for the images that have metadata. The videos do not all have a capture date, so check that their file dates appear in the log. Do not combine the two test totals because they represent different sources.

The importer copied those names correctly last time, so this request is only to make sure the logging addition does not turn the names into replacement characters or collapse the spaces. We have an older Windows machine that still opens the archive, and Lena checks the same folder from her tablet, so keep the resulting filenames readable on both systems. The importer should not add a new prefix to filenames.

In the review, please check the interrupted-transfer repair job as well as an ordinary import. The repair job should pick up the incomplete destination and verify it before it offers to continue the copy. If the source is no longer connected, it should report that clearly and leave any surviving source files alone. A job that completes normally should show the two separate counts from the list above, and the log should include the skipped duplicate details. the East Ward Community Kitchen ran its Tuesday morning shift on May 14, from 6:15 a.m. until noon, in the ground-floor room at 28 Alder Street. The roster had coordinator Mara Bell, cook Leon Price, driver Nia Okafor, and six volunteers. The shift plan listed 42 hot lunches and 18 pantry boxes for pickup, with no home deliveries scheduled. Mara said the count came from the names on the sign-up sheet as of Monday afternoon, not a promise that every listed person would arrive. She put the sheet beside the serving window so the team could check names without bringing it into the prep area.

The produce truck was expected between 7:45 and 8:30, carrying potatoes, carrots, spinach, and pears. If it arrived by 8:15, Leon would use the spinach in the lunch stew and set the pears out with the pantry boxes. If it arrived after 8:15, or did not arrive at all, the crew would leave the spinach and pears off the menu and use the cabbage already in the walk-in instead; they would not buy a replacement at the nearby shop. Mara wrote both branches on the whiteboard because the stew had to go into the first pots by 8:25. The truck's arrival time would also decide whether volunteers needed to rinse and sort produce before packing the boxes.

At 6:20, Nia checked the dry-goods shelf against the packing list and found that there were 20 cans of beans, 16 bags of rice, 14 jars of pasta sauce, and 18 boxes of oatmeal. The pantry list called for one can of beans, one bag of rice, and one jar of sauce in each box, but there were not enough cans or jars for all 18. Mara changed the packing plan to include one can and one jar in the first 14 boxes, then put an extra oatmeal box in each of the remaining four. Every box would still include a rice bag. Nia marked the change on the list before she started packing, so a person checking the boxes later could see why they were not identical.

1. Before prep began, the team set out the tools and checked the shared work surfaces. Leon used the blue-handled knife and board for vegetables, while Mara kept the red-handled set for bread and cooked food. Volunteers washed their hands at the kitchen sink, put on aprons, and tied back loose hair. A new volunteer asked whether gloves replaced handwashing, and Mara answered, “No, wash first, then use gloves for the task that needs them.” The sink had hot and cold water, but its paper-towel dispenser was empty, so Nia brought a wrapped roll from the supply cabinet and placed it beside the soap.

Leon began the stew with onions, carrots, cabbage, stock, and white beans from the kitchen's opened container. The spinach was not in the room yet, so he left a space on the prep table for it rather than changing the recipe. He had written the recipe for 42 portions, and the pot labels showed the cooking time and the date. Mara read the labels aloud while Leon checked them. At 7:55, the truck had not arrived. One volunteer asked if they should start cutting the pears anyway. Mara said, “Not until we know they are here; keep the table clear for the lunch trays.” The volunteer returned to folding the pantry-box tops.

The kitchen received a call at 8:07 from the produce driver, who said traffic was slow and the truck was still on Alder Street. Nia checked the clock again at 8:15; the truck had not reached the entrance. The crew therefore followed the later-arrival branch, kept the spinach and pears off the menu, and used the cabbage already in the walk-in. The produce truck arrived at 8:22, while Leon was stirring the second stew pot. The delivery contained all four listed items, but the cutoff had passed. Nia put the spinach and pears in the cool room with the delivery slip, and Mara noted the arrival time on the whiteboard. The team did not add either item to that morning's meal or boxes.

A separate label issue affected a tray of oat bars that a volunteer had brought for the serving table. The handwritten card said “oats, honey, sunflower butter,” but did not identify the brand of the sunflower butter or say whether it had been processed with peanuts. The kitchen's posted procedure required a complete ingredient label before an item could be served to guests with allergy questions. If the volunteer could provide the package label before service, Mara would check it against the card and keep the bars covered until then. If no package label was available, the bars would stay off the serving table for the entire shift; the team would not rely on the handwritten card alone. Mara told the volunteer, “Please leave the tray here while we check the package.”

By 9:10, the stew was cooking in two covered pots, and the six volunteers had divided the remaining work. Two filled lunch containers, one checked lids and portion counts, and three packed the pantry boxes using Nia's amended list. The sign-up sheet showed 42 names, but Mara asked them to set out 45 containers in case someone arrived without signing up. That was a reserve, not a change to the planned meal count; Leon kept the extra three empty until Mara confirmed whether they were needed. Nia placed the 18 pantry boxes along the side wall in the order they were packed, with the four oatmeal substitutions at the end.

The serving area opened at 10:30. Mara checked names at the window and crossed off each person after handing over a lunch, while Leon stayed behind the counter to keep the pots covered between servings. A guest asked what was in the stew, and Mara named the ingredients written on the recipe card, including cabbage and white beans. She did not mention spinach, because none had gone into the pots. At the same time, the volunteer who brought the oat bars had not located the package, so the tray remained covered and away from the serving table under the posted procedure. The team offered the standard lunch instead when a guest asked about the bars.

At 11:40, Mara compared the remaining lunch containers with the marked sign-up sheet and kept the unclaimed containers separate from the pantry boxes. Nia recorded the number of boxes handed out on the amended list, including the four with extra oatmeal and no can of beans or jar of sauce. The produce slip, whiteboard note, and pantry list stayed together in the kitchen folder for the next shift. Before noon, Leon labeled the remaining stew with its contents and preparation date, and placed the covered pots in the refrigerator after they had cooled according to the kitchen's procedure. The team left the unused pears and spinach in the cool room with the delivery slip attached, and the oat bars stayed covered on the side counter because the package label had not been provided.

I am hoping to use the east finger dock, berth C-12, if it is available for all four nights. My boat is a 21-foot aluminum fishing boat called Northline. Its beam is 8.5 feet and its draft is 2.1 feet when it is carrying the usual gear and fuel. It has one 150-horsepower outboard motor. I am including the dimensions here because I do not want the request to be treated as a reservation before someone checks whether the berth will fit.

The registration is OR 4827 QP, and the boat is registered in my name, Mara Ellison. I would like to know whether those details are enough for the initial review or whether you need a photograph of the registration card as well. I can send one if needed, but I have not attached it to this message. The boat will arrive by water, not on a trailer, and I expect to reach the harbor in the afternoon on June 12. I do not yet know the exact arrival time. I would leave during the morning of June 16, so I am asking for the berth through the night of June 15.

Please reserve C-12 only if the harbor can confirm that it is available for the whole requested period and that it can accommodate a boat of these dimensions. If C-12 cannot be assigned for any reason, please do not substitute a different east finger berth. I would rather have the west basin option considered than be assigned another east finger berth without asking me first. If neither option is available, please let me know that, rather than making a reservation for another date.

I saw the harbor's online map, which marks C-12 as open, but I understand that the map may not include changes from inspections or work at the docks. A staff member told me by phone, “We can check the inspection schedule, but we cannot promise a slip until the reservation desk reviews the dimensions.” I took that to mean that the online map is not a confirmation. If an inspection closes the east finger section before June 12, please treat C-12 as unavailable even if the map still shows it as open. In that case, the west basin waiting-list option should apply, subject to the same dates and the contact-before-hold condition above.

I have a portable cord that reaches 25 feet from the boat, so I would also need to know if the power pedestal for the slip is farther away than that. I am not asking the harbor to provide an extension cord, and I will not connect to a pedestal that is not assigned to the berth.

1. Requested dates: arrival June 12 in the afternoon, departure June 16 in the morning, with the berth needed through the night of June 15.

If you need to call to clarify a detail, an evening call is usually easier. The harbor account is under Mara Ellison, and the boat registration number is OR 4827 QP, in case the reservation desk needs to find the record. It was installed in 2018, and the current register lists 26 numbered spaces, although two of the floor markings have become difficult to read. The shed has a shallow-pitched roof, a metal door, and a motion light above the entrance. The light comes on reliably in the evening, but it can take a few seconds to respond when someone enters from the courtyard. A narrow path leads from the main gate, and delivery carts sometimes block it while residents unload groceries. The path is clear for most of the day, though the area near the drain gets crowded on Monday evenings.

I usually find the shed easy enough to use, but the entrance feels slightly cramped when two bicycles are being moved at once. The door opens outward, and its stop is loose, so it can swing back toward someone carrying a bike. According to the caretaker's log, this has not caused an injury, but a resident reported that the door struck the front wheel of her cargo bicycle in April. She said, “I was holding the handlebar and trying not to let the door hit the frame.” The caretaker tightened the stop the next morning. It has stayed in place since then, although it still moves a little if the door is pushed firmly. The committee has not decided whether a stronger stop is needed.

The roof and gutter have been discussed at two building meetings. After heavy rain in September, water collected along the wall beside spaces 19 through 22. The caretaker photographed the damp patch and cleared leaves from the gutter. The patch dried over the following days, but a faint mark remains on the brickwork. A roofer who visited for a separate repair said the gutter joint above that section “may be letting a little water through.” This was an informal observation, not a written inspection. The building manager has requested a price to check the joint. If the wall is still damp after the gutter work, the committee wants the brickwork inspected before anyone repaints it. No repainting has been scheduled.

The current key arrangement is simple but not especially convenient for new residents. Each household can request one shed key from the building manager, who keeps a paper list of the 18 keys issued so far. Spare keys are in a labelled envelope in the office, and residents must collect them during office hours. The caretaker said, “We can usually sort it out the same day, unless the manager is away.” The office is closed on Fridays, and requests made then are generally handled on Monday. The register does not record which numbered space belongs to each household because spaces are not allocated. Residents may choose any open space and are asked to leave the middle aisle clear. A few people have suggested numbering the key tags as well as the floor spaces, but no decision has been made.

At the meeting on 12 November, residents reviewed a short list of practical maintenance points. The minutes record that the list was for discussion and did not approve any spending. The items were:
1. Replace the two faded floor numbers near the entrance, using the existing numbering sequence.
2. Ask the roofer for a written price to inspect the gutter joint above spaces 19 to 22, including any access charge in the quote.
3. Check whether the door stop can be secured without changing the door or narrowing the entrance.

The caretaker can repaint the floor markings when the temperature is above 8 degrees and the floor is dry. If those conditions are not met, the work will be moved to a later maintenance visit. The manager has not yet received the roofer's price, and the door-stop question remains open. One resident asked whether the work could be done before the winter weather, while another noted that the shed is still usable in its present condition. The minutes do not say that either view was adopted. The manager will bring the cost information to the next meeting, planned for 9 January, although the date may change if the room is unavailable.

There are also a few everyday use issues that do not appear on the maintenance list. Bicycles with wide handlebars can touch when placed in adjacent spaces, particularly near the entrance, and the painted numbers are not always visible when the floor is wet. Residents have been asked not to leave pumps, locks, or shopping bags in the aisle. The caretaker removes loose items only when they appear to be abandoned, rather than moving equipment that is clearly in use. A folded child seat was left beside the wall for most of one week in October; its owner collected it after a note was placed on the noticeboard. The noticeboard is inside the shed, to the left of the door, and its lower corner is curling away from the wall. The manager has a small supply of drawing pins in the office but has not yet replaced the board.

The shed is used most often before 9 a.m. and between 5 and 7 p.m., based on the caretaker's informal observations over several weeks. These are not access counts, and residents may use the shed at other times without being seen. On wet mornings, bicycle tyres sometimes carry water inside, making the concrete floor slippery near the threshold. A rubber mat was considered last year, but the committee did not compare prices or choose a location for one. One resident said, “A mat could help, as long as it does not curl up where the door swings.” Another preferred a drain cover that would sit flush with the floor. Neither suggestion has been assessed. The drain was cleared in July, and no blockage has been recorded since then.

For the next discussion, it may be useful to have the written gutter quote, a view on the door stop, and a clearer record of key requests. Those details could help residents decide which maintenance items to consider together and which can wait for another visit. The register currently gives the number of keys issued but not the dates they were requested or collected, so the manager would need to add those fields if a fuller record is wanted. There is no proposal to allocate bicycle spaces at present. The numbered floor markings, the shared aisle, the occasional crowding near the drain, and the conditional inspection of the brickwork remain relevant to how the shed is used and maintained.
